summary.value: This paper addresses text spotting in complex artistic images by fine-tuning multimodal LLMs with a joint SFT+RL approach. It introduces SupGRPO, which integrates GRPO with a matching-based online SFT applied only to coordinate tokens, mitigating GRPO’s reward sparsity for localization and SFT’s instance-order dependency (Fig. 1b, Sec. 3.3). The GRPO side uses four rule-based rewards—format, word-level text F1, IoU precision, and IoU recall—to align training with non-differentiable evaluation metrics (Sec. 3.2, Fig. 2). Matching for SFT supervises coordinates only when predicted and ground-truth text match and IoU > 0, and the combined loss is given in Eq. (10). The authors also curate ATS, an artistic text spotting dataset with 6.5k training and 2.5k test images, annotated with word-level quadrilateral boxes and transcriptions (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 3). Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL (3B/7B) and Qwen3-VL-8B show that SupGRPO improves both recognition and detection over SFT-only, GRPO-only, and a two-stage SFT→GRPO baseline across Total-Text, ICDAR15, CTW1500, and ATS (Tabs. 1–3), with ablations confirming complementary effects of SFT (detection) and GRPO (recognition) (Sec. 4.4, Tabs. 5–8).

strengths.value:
1. Clear, original training paradigm that couples RL with targeted SFT. SupGRPO integrates GRPO with a matching-based online SFT applied only to coordinate tokens (Sec. 3.3, Eq. (9)–(10), Fig. 2), directly addressing two concrete issues: GRPO’s reward sparsity for localization and standard SFT’s instance order dependency (Fig. 1b).

2. Task-aligned reward design. The four rewards—format, word-level content F1, IoU precision, IoU recall—are carefully motivated to match non-differentiable evaluation metrics (Sec. 3.2). The rationale for choosing word-level F1 over soft metrics (ANLS/Edit Distance) and the multiset handling of duplicates to penalize hallucinated repeats are thoughtful and practically important (Eq. (6)).

3. Evidence-backed decomposition of detection vs. recognition gains. The paper establishes a non-trivial empirical insight—“SFT yields more significant improvements in text detection… whereas GRPO provides a more substantial boost to text recognition” (Sec. 4.4, Tab. 5)—and then capitalizes on it with a joint objective (Eq. (10)) that materially improves both.

4. Strong, consistent, and broad empirical improvements. SupGRPO outperforms SFT-only, GRPO-only, and two-stage SFT→GRPO across four datasets and multiple base models (Tabs. 1–3). Notably large gains on ATS recognition and detection (Tab. 1, Tab. 2), validating the approach in the intended hard regime.

5. Thorough ablations that isolate design choices. The paper dissects token-level supervision (all/text/location tokens) and shows that supervising only location tokens with matching is best for joint performance (Sec. 4.4, Tab. 6–7). It also demonstrates that separating precision and recall rewards is superior to a single F1 reward for detection (Tab. 8).

6. Effective matching criterion for online SFT. The combined text+IoU matching used to supervise coordinates outperforms IoU-only and text-only alternatives (Sec. 4.4, Tab. 7), providing concrete evidence that the matching strategy is crucial rather than incidental.

7. Training stability improvements are quantified. SupGRPO yields higher and smoother reward curves and lower, more stable loss than vanilla GRPO (App. Fig. 5), supporting the claim that online SFT regularizes exploration updates.

8. Practical engineering that improves parseability and evaluation. The format reward (Sec. 3.2) ensures outputs are structurally valid JSON-like lists, which is a pragmatic and often overlooked necessity for RL fine-tuning of MLLMs on structured tasks.

9. Demonstrated scalability and generality. The method works across Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B and Qwen3-VL-8B (Sec. 4.2; Tabs. 1–3), and scaling to 8B narrows the detection gap to specialized spotters (e.g., ATS 86.2 vs. ABCNet v2 87.5 in Tab. 2; Total-Text/IC15 in Tab. 3).

10. New, targeted benchmark with clear characterization. ATS specifically targets artistic text, is non-trivial in size (6.5k/2.5k), and is well described with qualitative exemplars (Fig. 3) and distribution statistics (App. Fig. 4). It fills a gap not captured by standard scene-text sets (Sec. 4.1).

11. Reproducibility-oriented presentation. The method is specified with concrete equations (Sec. 3.1–3.3), explicit hyperparameters (Sec. 4.2: LoRA, batch size, G=8 samples, β=0.04, λ=1e-4), training data composition (~30k samples), and open-source training frameworks (Open-R1/VLM-R1), facilitating reimplementation.

12. Compelling qualitative behaviors. Visuals show better localization than MLLMs and broader recognition coverage than specialized spotters, including multilingual spotting and plausible completion under occlusion (App. Fig. 6), reinforcing the quantitative claims.

weaknesses.value:
1. Recognition comparisons mix incompatible protocols, conflating conclusions. In Sec. 4.3 and Tab. 1, specialized spotters are scored only when detection is correct (detection-coupled), while MLLMs are scored on recognition from the whole image “even if the specific localization … is less precise.” This favors MLLMs and makes cross-family rankings hard to interpret. Actionable: add an end-to-end spotting metric that requires joint box+text correctness for all methods (e.g., IoU ≥ 0.5 and exact text match via bipartite matching), and report both detection-free recognition and detection-coupled recognition for MLLMs.

2. Reward decomposition is misaligned with true end-to-end objectives. Sec. 3.2 optimizes text F1 over a bag-of-words and detection precision/recall over IoU matches independently. This allows progress on boxes without correct text (and vice versa), whereas standard end-to-end spotting requires a joint match. Actionable: introduce an instance-level, bipartite-matched spotting reward that scores a pair only when both IoU and text are correct (e.g., per-pair reward of 1 if IoU ≥ τ and text exact match, else 0), or a weighted version that combines IoU and exact/near-exact text. Compare against the current “Text + P + R” reward in Tab. 8.

3. Missing permutation-invariant SFT baselines. The central argument against standard SFT is “instance order dependency” (Fig. 1b, Sec. 3.3). However, the paper does not test order-agnostic SFT trained with matching (Hungarian) over predicted/GT instances—common in DETR-style models (Carion et al., 2020; TESTR, Zhang et al., 2022). Actionable: implement a permutation-invariant SFT baseline that supervises both text and coordinates after bipartite matching, and compare it against SupGRPO to establish the necessity of RL.

4. No sensitivity analysis of key couplings/thresholds. The combined loss weight λ in Eq. (10) is fixed to 1e-4; β (KL in Eq. (1)) is 0.04; GRPO uses G=8 samples (Sec. 4.2). The matching IoU threshold is inconsistent—“IoU > 0” in Sec. 3.3 versus 0.3 in Sec. 4.4/Tab. 7. Actionable: (a) report performance vs. λ, β, G, and the matching IoU threshold; (b) standardize and justify the chosen IoU threshold; (c) consider curriculum/schedules for λ to reduce interference between RL and SFT.

5. Coordinate-only SFT leaves recognition to sparse RL signals. Ablations (Tab. 7) show “+ Text Tokens SFT” boosts recognition (84.1) but hurts detection (60.8). The current choice avoids text SFT altogether, likely underutilizing supervised signals for hard texts. Actionable: devise a permutation-invariant text SFT (via matching) and explore gated/coordinated weighting so text-token SFT does not suppress detection (e.g., alternate updates, uncertainty-aware weights, or text-SFT only on high-IoU matches). Report the accuracy/efficiency trade-off.

6. Limited reporting on computational efficiency and stability beyond curves. While App. Fig. 5 shows smoother rewards/losses for SupGRPO, there is no wall-clock, GPU-hours, or throughput comparison against SFT-only and GRPO-only, nor sample-efficiency metrics. Actionable: report training time, GPU budget, and inference latency for TS-VL-3B/7B/8B; include convergence speed (steps to target F1) to substantiate claims that SupGRPO is “more stable and efficient.”

7. ATS dataset documentation is insufficient for assessing quality and potential bias. Sec. 4.1 and App. Fig. 4 give distributions, but there is no annotation protocol, inter-annotator agreement, de-duplication across train/test, or license/source attributions for re-use from TextSeg/WAS. Actionable: add (a) QA procedures and spot-check error rates; (b) near-duplicate analysis across splits; (c) guidelines for text normalization (case, punctuation); (d) licensing and ethical sourcing; and (e) style/category tags to enable stratified evaluation.

8. Generalization to unseen artistic styles is not stress-tested. Tab. 4 shows that adding ATS to training improves ATS test performance, but does not quantify robustness to new artistic distributions. Actionable: perform leave-one-style-out evaluations within ATS, or train without ATS and test on ATS subsets grouped by style/complexity (Fig. 3 categories), to measure true cross-domain robustness.

9. Ambiguity in detection metrics and thresholds undermines reproducibility and comparability. Tabs. 2–3 report a single “Detection” score without specifying IoU threshold(s), matching (one-to-one/greedy), or whether transcription correctness is required (Sec. 4.3 implies not). Actionable: (a) specify detection metric details; (b) add PR curves or AP at multiple IoUs; (c) report an end-to-end detection+recognition score on the same protocol.

10. Two-stage baselines are narrow. Only SFT→GRPO is tested (Tabs. 1–3), but not GRPO→SFT or alternating schedules that might preserve SFT’s localization while leveraging GRPO’s recognition gains. Actionable: add GRPO→SFT and interleaved schedules; report where they fail/succeed relative to SupGRPO to strengthen the joint-training claim.

11. Reward design for text may still encourage undesirable behaviors. Although Sec. 3.2 uses multisets to penalize hallucinated duplicates, bag-of-words F1 disregards word order and grouping, which are crucial in artistic compositions (Sec. 4.1). Actionable: augment text rewards with instance-level correctness via matching, or incorporate phrase-level rewards (e.g., bigram F1) to discourage shuffling/hallucination while keeping non-differentiability aligned with evaluation.

questions.value:
1. Evaluation protocol for recognition (Sec. 4.3; Tab. 1).  
   - Can you add an end-to-end spotting metric for all methods that requires joint correctness (IoU ≥ τ plus exact text via bipartite matching) so specialized spotters and MLLMs are directly comparable? Please report both the current “recognition from the full image” and a detection-coupled recognition for MLLMs. This could change the interpretation of Tab. 1.

2. Reward alignment with end-to-end objectives (Sec. 3.2; Eq. (6)–(8)).  
   - Your rewards decompose text (bag-of-words F1) and detection (IoU precision/recall). Did you try an instance-level, bipartite-matched reward that grants credit only when both IoU ≥ τ and text match exactly? A comparison against “Text & P & R” in Tab. 8 would clarify whether joint scoring improves policy learning.

3. Permutation-invariant SFT baseline (Sec. 3.3; Fig. 1b).  
   - The order-dependency critique of standard SFT is central. Could you include a DETR-style, permutation-invariant SFT baseline that supervises both text and coordinates after Hungarian matching between predicted and GT instances? If this narrows the gap to SupGRPO, it would calibrate the necessity of RL.

4. Matching threshold inconsistency (Sec. 3.3 vs. Sec. 4.4/Tab. 7).  
   - Sec. 3.3 states “IoU > 0” for matches used in L_SFT-coord (Eq. (9)), while Tab. 7 uses 0.3 for IoU-based matching. What threshold is used in SupGRPO training? Please standardize and provide sensitivity to the threshold.

5. Sensitivity of key hyperparameters (Eq. (10); Sec. 4.2).  
   - Please report performance vs λ (set to 1e-4), β in Eq. (1) (0.04), the GRPO group size G (8), and decoding parameters during sampling. Also clarify which π_ref you use (Fig. 2) and whether β is fixed or adaptive. This will increase confidence in robustness.

6. Coordinate-only SFT choice (Sec. 3.3; Tab. 7).  
   - “+ Text Tokens SFT” improves recognition but hurts detection. Have you tried text-token SFT after matching (i.e., supervise text only for high-IoU matches), alternating updates (e.g., text-SFT every k steps), or uncertainty/gating to avoid suppressing detection? A small study here could reveal a better recognition–detection trade-off.

7. Detection metric details (Tabs. 2–3).  
   - Please specify IoU thresholds, one-to-one vs. greedy matching, and whether transcription is ignored for detection scoring. Adding PR curves or AP at multiple IoUs (e.g., 0.5/0.75) would make comparisons clearer and aid reproducibility.

8. ATS dataset documentation (Sec. 4.1; Fig. 3; App. Fig. 4).  
   - Can you detail the annotation protocol, QA (spot-check error rates, inter-annotator agreement), de-duplication across train/test, text normalization (case, punctuation), language coverage, and licensing/source attributions from TextSeg and WAS? This is critical for assessing bias and reusability.

9. Generalization to unseen styles (Sec. 4.1; Fig. 3).  
   - Beyond Tab. 4’s “with/without ATS,” could you provide stratified results by ATS categories (overlap, irregular arrangement, complex scenes) or a leave-one-style-out evaluation? This would test the claim that MLLM reasoning helps on novel artistic layouts.

10. Two-stage and interleaved schedules (Sec. 4.3; Tabs. 1–3).  
    - You evaluate SFT → GRPO. What about GRPO → SFT or interleaving (e.g., alternating epochs)? If these underperform SupGRPO, brief evidence would strengthen the joint-training argument.

11. Credit assignment granularity in GRPO (Sec. 3.1; Eq. (2)).  
    - Advantages are sequence-level and applied uniformly to all tokens. Did you explore per-instance or per-span weighting (e.g., higher weight on coordinate tokens or on matched instances) to tighten credit assignment? Any preliminary findings would clarify whether finer-grained shaping helps.

12. Handling unmatched predictions in online SFT (Sec. 3.3; Eq. (9)).  
    - Unmatched predicted boxes seem to receive no SFT signal. Did you consider “no-object” negatives or contrastive penalties for unmatched coordinate tokens to discourage spurious boxes?

13. Text reward normalization and multilingual cases (Eq. (6); App. Fig. 6).  
    - How are case, punctuation, Unicode normalization, and tokenization handled for word-level F1, especially for non-space-delimited scripts (e.g., Chinese in Fig. 6)? A precise definition will help others reproduce your scores.

14. Computational budget and efficiency (Sec. 4.2; App. Fig. 5).  
    - Please report wall-clock training time, GPU-hours, and convergence steps for SFT-only, GRPO-only, and SupGRPO on 3B/7B/8B, plus inference latency/memory. This would substantiate the “more stable and efficient” learning claim suggested by Fig. 5.

15. Format reward ablation and parseability (Sec. 3.2; Fig. 2).  
    - How often do generated sequences violate the required structure over training, and how much does the format reward contribute to final metrics? A small ablation or a plot of parse success rate would clarify its necessity.

16. Catastrophic forgetting (Sec. D).  
    - Could you quantify the reported “slight degradation” on standard multimodal benchmarks and show whether LoRA rank/target layers modulate this trade-off? A table with before/after scores would make the limitation more concrete.

17. Reproducibility details (Sec. 4.2).  
    - Please provide LoRA config (rank/alpha/target modules), seeds, prompt templates, coordinate tokenization/quantization scheme (e.g., range, precision, rounding), and decoding settings used during GRPO sampling and evaluation. These specifics can materially affect results.

18. Release plan.  
    - Confirm that ATS (with licenses/attributions) and code will be released upon acceptance, and whether evaluation scripts for rewards and metrics will be included to ensure comparability.
